title: AgentCraft: Putting the Orc in Orchestration — Ido Salomon

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 67%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is multi-agent orchestration patterns, harness design, and the control plane for coordinating many parallel coding agents. AgentCraft directly orchestrates coding agents like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex in software-engineering contexts. The presenter describes AgentCraft as free, experimental, and actively seeking community feedback via Discord. The talk assumes prior familiarity with coding agents and introduces moderate orchestration concepts. A conference presentation at the AI Engineer channel featuring live product demonstrations. All evidence anchors are graded said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the transcript.

summary: Ido Salomon opens by noting that while agents are powerful, scaling to dozens of agents fails because humans become the orchestration bottleneck. Managing dozens of reckless agents isn't a typical engineering skill, but analogous skills exist in unexpected places—particularly real-time strategy (RTS) games, where players manage dozens of units. AgentCraft is built on this insight, transferring gaming learnings into productivity. The demo begins with a physical agent representation—a live coding session (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, etc.) detectable on the device, visualized, and spawnable directly from the UI. Users can prompt agents via voice, text, or images. The UI includes buildings representing functionality like skills/plugins management, an integrated terminal, and git for end-to-end workflows. Visibility is the second pillar: a side panel shows high-level mission status, and the map is a projection of the user's file system—directories and files appear as rooms, allowing users to visually track which file each agent works on, see full change lists, and maintain lineage. A heat map visualizes and can proactively prevent file collisions. Reacting quickly leverages RTS muscle memory to cycle between agents needing approval or answers. But this alone only enables short bursts of parallel agent use. To sustain it, AgentCraft introduces quests (agents find missions for the user), campaigns (users give broad ideas, agents decompose and plan in containers, a campaign orchestrator handles babysitting), review bundles with visual evidence (screenshots, videos), and cron-based autonomous agents (e.g., scanning Twitter for ideas and implementing them). The talk emphasizes shifting effort from planning to review—running tasks ten times and picking the best. For human collaboration, shared workspaces let teammates see each other's agents, hand off work, and collaborate via a chat mechanism between humans and agents, with agents aware of who else is working on files for soft collaboration. Salomon concludes these aren't new skills—just unused for work until now—and invites the audience to try AgentCraft (free, experimental) and join the Discord.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Problem Statement
sections.summary: Salomon introduces himself as creator of AgentCraft, MC I, and MC apps. He poses the question of why we don't scale to 100 agents for 100x productivity, and identifies the core problem: humans are the bottleneck in orchestrating agents. He connects this to RTS gaming, where managing dozens of units is already familiar.

sections.title: AgentCraft Basics: Agents & Buildings
sections.summary: Demo begins with a physical agent representation—a live coding session detectable and spawnable from the UI. Users can prompt via voice, text, or images. Buildings in the UI represent functionality: skills/plugins management, integrated terminal, and git for end-to-end workflow.

sections.title: Visibility: File System Map & Heat Maps
sections.summary: A side panel shows high-level mission status. The map is a projection of the file system—directories and files appear as rooms, letting users visually track which file each agent works on with full change lists and agent lineage. A heat map visualizes and can proactively prevent file collisions.

sections.title: Reacting: Muscle Memory & Initial Limits
sections.summary: RTS-style muscle memory enables quick cycling between agents needing approval or answers. Salomon notes this only solves the first step—parallel agent use is sustainable only for short bursts due to limited human idea capacity and babysitting overhead.

sections.title: Overcoming Limits: Quests & Campaigns
sections.summary: Quests let agents find missions for the user. Campaigns let users give broad ideas; agents decompose, plan, and run in containers while a campaign orchestrator handles babysitting, shifting human effort to planning and review phases only.

sections.title: Autonomous Agents & Review Bundles
sections.summary: Cron-based autonomous agents can scan Twitter for ideas and implement them—this is how 'channels' was built. Review bundles show changes with visual evidence (screenshots, videos), enabling a shift from planning to review by running tasks multiple times and picking the best.

sections.title: Human Collaboration & Workspaces
sections.summary: Shared workspaces let teammates (e.g., a product designer) see each other's agents, hand off work, and collaborate. A chat mechanism enables both human-human and human-agent communication, with agents aware of who else is working on files for soft collaboration.

sections.title: Conclusion & Call to Action
sections.summary: Salomon concludes these orchestration skills aren't new—they've been used in gaming but not for work. AgentCraft aims to raise the human-agent collaboration ceiling via visibility, autonomy, and collaboration. He invites the audience to download the free experimental tool and join the Discord for feedback.
